# Jung — The Undiscovered Self (Routledge, 2013)

## Essay use

Jung supplies the psychological hinge between mass-mindedness and political capture: the individual reduced to an abstract social unit, responsibility delegated to a collective body, and the State hypostatised as a quasi-personality manipulable by particular people.

**Claim boundary:** Jung's religious counterweight and his historical diagnosis remain his own psychological argument. The essay's `0/1 ↔ 1/0` political third, syn-ballein method, and institutional praxis are argued QL extensions.

## Verified passage

Chapter 1, "The Plight of the Individual in Modern Society," p. 10: **“The bigger the crowd, the more negligible the individual becomes.”** The sentence carries the precise psychological hinge required here: mass is not merely many people, but a condition in which the individual is rendered negligible. It does not establish the QL matheme or collapse the institutional analysis into psychology.

The complete, context-preserving sequence—statistical abstraction, crowd diminution, delegated responsibility, and State hypostasis—is in [Quotes — Jung, The Undiscovered Self (Routledge, 2013)](#passages).

## Passage sequence: the mass-State circuit

<a id="jung-2013-undiscovered-self-routledge-jus-01"></a>
### JUS-01 — Statistical abstraction

**Locator:** chapter 1, pp. 9–10.

**Provenance:** paraphrase checked against the selected Routledge Great Minds edition; no quoted wording is claimed for this card.

Jung argues that scientific rationalism can make the individual appear as an abstract social unit: a statistical instance, exchangeable and externally measured. The claim is not that number or science is inherently tyrannical; it is that the average becomes politically dangerous when it replaces the irreducible person as the real unit of judgment.

**Use in the essay:** This is the psychological face of the dia cut: a living `1` is detached from the relations through which it is concrete, then rendered administrable as an isolated number.

<a id="jung-2013-undiscovered-self-routledge-jus-02"></a>
### JUS-02 — Crowd diminution

**Locator:** chapter 1, p. 10.

> “The bigger the crowd, the more negligible the individual becomes.”

The line follows Jung's discussion of the individual overwhelmed by scale, statistical reality, and collective force. It does not condemn every collective; it names the threshold at which numerical magnitude becomes a substitute for judgment and individual responsibility.

**Use in the essay:** Le Bon gives the emergent crowd; Jung names the subjective cost. Together they make mass formation a transformation of relation, not a mere aggregation of people.

<a id="jung-2013-undiscovered-self-routledge-jus-03"></a>
### JUS-03 — Delegated responsibility

**Locator:** chapter 1, p. 11.

> “responsibility is collectivized as much as possible”

Jung's immediate context is the individual who transfers responsibility to a corporate body. Society is then no longer understood as a relation sustained by persons; it is hypostatised as an agent that can relieve persons of judgment.

**Use in the essay:** This is the middle operation between dia and monopoly: the local authority is permitted to occupy the slash because the persons whose relation it administers have surrendered the return-path.

<a id="jung-2013-undiscovered-self-routledge-jus-04"></a>
### JUS-04 — State hypostasis and manipulation

**Locator:** chapter 1, p. 11.

> “The State in particular is turned into a quasi-animate personality.”

Jung immediately qualifies the false personhood: it is a camouflage for the people who know how to manipulate the apparatus. This is the needed hinge between psychic mass formation and concrete power; the State is neither an autonomous subject nor reducible to a crowd, but an apparatus that can be personified and operated.

**Use in the essay:** The passage stops the mass-formation account becoming politically innocent. It carries the essay from mass capture to the institution/citizen and empire/subject relations through which capture is reproduced.

## Argument boundary

Jung supplies a psychological diagnosis of modern mass-mindedness. The essay's further claim—that `0/1 ↔ 1/0` is the transcendental third by which divided positions may **divine and concur**—is an argued QL extension. It is neither a quotation from Jung nor a replacement for institutional analysis.
